planting.note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before last frost, or divide established clumps in spring, and set out after frost danger passes into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade.

directions: Set out divisions or transplants in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade, spacing plants 12–18 inches apart, and pinch stems through early summer to build bushy, floriferous plants. Chrysanthemum indicum is the wild East Asian species behind centuries of chrysanthemum tea (ju hua cha) and one of the parents of the modern florist mum, bearing masses of small, single, bright yellow daisy flowers on wiry stems from late summer into fall. Harvest flowers just as they open and air- or oven-dry them for tea, or leave them standing for pollinators — hoverflies and late-season bees depend on the nectar when little else is blooming. Divide congested clumps every 2–3 years in spring to keep plants vigorous and floriferous.

planting.note: Set out rooted transplants after all frost danger has passed into moderately fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; most gardeners buy started plants since named color strains are propagated by cuttings.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil after frost danger passes, and deadhead spent flowers regularly to keep the mounding plants covered in bloom from spring through fall. Native to the Canary Islands, the Marguerite daisy produces an abundance of single or double, white, pink, or yellow daisy flowers with cheerful golden centers over finely cut, gray-green foliage, making it a workhorse for containers, window boxes, and border edges. It flowers most heavily in cool-to-mild weather and can slow in the hardest summer heat, reviving again as temperatures ease in fall; shear plants back by a third if they become leggy to prompt fresh growth and bloom. Hardy as a woody perennial only in zones 9–11, it is grown everywhere else as a fast, reliable warm-season annual.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in very well-drained soil in full sun; euryops is nearly always propagated vegetatively rather than from seed.

directions: Plant in full sun in fast-draining soil, spacing plants 24–36 inches apart, and shear lightly after each bloom flush to keep the rounded mound tidy and dense. Native to South Africa, euryops daisy is a fine-textured, silvery-gray-leaved shrub that produces bright golden-yellow, 2-inch daisy flowers almost continuously in mild climates, with the heaviest flush in fall through spring and lighter bloom through summer heat. It is highly drought- and salt-tolerant once established, making it a mainstay of Gulf Coast and coastal landscaping, and is largely untroubled by pests or disease as long as drainage is sharp — soggy soil is its main weakness. Hardy as a perennial shrub only in zones 9–11; further north it is grown as a container plant brought indoors before frost or replaced annually as a warm-season bedding plant.

planting.note: Sow indoors 6–8 weeks before last frost or plant divisions in spring in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun; Gold Plate needs excellent drainage and resents heavy, wet clay.

directions: Plant in lean, very well-drained soil in full sun, staking in windy sites if needed to keep the tall stems upright, and cut flower heads for fresh or dried arrangements just as they fully open. Gold Plate is a classic straight-species selection of the Caucasus native Achillea filipendulina, distinguished from hybrid yarrows by its exceptionally large, flat, mustard-gold flower heads — often 5–6 inches across — held well above ferny, aromatic, gray-green foliage on sturdy stems. It is among the tallest garden yarrows, valued for the back of the border and for cutting gardens, and its dried flower heads hold color for months. Extremely drought- and heat-tolerant once established; divide congested clumps every 2–3 years in spring to maintain vigor and flower size.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring with the crown at soil level in fertile, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun with roots kept cool by mulch or low companion plants.

directions: Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun with the roots shaded and cool, and stake loosely or let plants sprawl through neighboring perennials since this species has no tendrils to climb with. Unlike its vining relatives, Clematis integrifolia is a true herbaceous perennial that forms an upright to sprawling clump of un-lobed leaves topped from early to midsummer with nodding, bell-shaped, deep blue-violet flowers with distinctively twisted, recurved petal tips. It combines beautifully at the front to middle of a mixed border, weaving through roses and other perennials for support, and makes an excellent, long-lasting cut flower both in bloom and as fluffy silvery seed heads afterward. Cut the entire plant back to a few inches in late winter, since it blooms on new growth each year.
